title: What Excel is for
summary: Workbooks, sheets and cells, and the real jobs that run on Excel.
objectives: Name the parts of a workbook: sheets, columns, rows, cells and ranges.
Read and write a cell address like **D4** and a range like **A1:E6**.
Say which everyday jobs Excel does well, and when another tool fits better.

slides.h: Excel is a grid of cells that can calculate
p: An Excel file is called a **workbook**. Inside it are **worksheets**, the grids you see, each with its own tab at the bottom.
Every box in the grid is a **cell**. You can type text, numbers or dates into a cell, or a **formula** that works something out from other cells.

visual.caption: A workbook with three sheets. The active cell is D4.

callouts.text: The Name Box shows the address

slides.h: Columns are letters, rows are numbers
p: Columns run down and are named A, B, C … After Z comes AA, AB and so on, up to XFD: 16,384 columns. Rows run across and are numbered 1 to 1,048,576.
A cell’s address is its column letter, then its row number: **D4** is column D, row 4. That address is how formulas point at cells.

head: You see
It means
rows: Every cell from A1 to E6: a block of 5 columns × 6 rows
Cell D8 on the sheet called Orders

slides.h: A range is a block of cells
p: A **range** is a rectangle of cells, written as its first and last cell with a colon between: `A1:E6`.
Most of Excel’s work happens on ranges: you format them, sort them and add them up. When you drag across cells, you are selecting a range.

check.q: Which address means column C, row 12?
check.explain: Column letter first, then the row number: **C12**.

why.0: Excel puts the column letter first.
why.2: A colon joins two cells into a range; it doesn’t belong inside one address.
why.3: That’s an older style some people switch on; normal Excel shows C12.

lecture.title: What people actually use it for

slides.h: The jobs that run on Excel
p: Budgets, sales trackers, attendance, stock lists, invoices, fee registers, project plans, survey results, salary sheets and dashboards all run on Excel in offices across India.
Any time you have rows of things with the same details for each (a list of orders, each with a date, customer and amount), Excel is a natural fit.

head: Job
What Excel does
rows: Totals, differences, a chart of where money goes
Sort by amount, filter by city, sum by month

p: Excel is not a word processor: long letters belong in Word. It is not a database for millions of records shared by hundreds of people at once. And it is not a design tool.
A good test: if your information is a **table of facts** you want to sort, count or calculate, use Excel.

bad.title: Wrong tool
bad.text: A 4-page letter typed into cells, one sentence per row.

good.title: Right tool
good.text: A list of 200 orders with date, customer, city and amount, totalled by city.

check.q: Which of these suits Excel best?
options: A list of 300 students with marks in five subjects
check.explain: Rows of the same details for each item, plus calculations: that’s Excel’s home ground.

steps.say: Click a cell to make it active. This is **A1**, the top-left corner.
Column D, row 4: cell **D4** holds Neha’s order amount. The Name Box at the top left always shows the active cell’s address.
Drag from A1 to E6 to select a **range**. Every order, every column.
Cell **D8** holds a formula. The grid shows its result; the formula bar shows `=SUM(D2:D6)`.
Sheet tabs at the bottom switch between worksheets. This is the **Customers** sheet.

demo.outro: Cells, ranges and sheets: that’s the whole map. Now you find your way around.

quiz.q: An Excel file is called a…
quiz.explain: The file is the workbook; the grids inside are worksheets.

quiz.q: How many cells are in the range B2:C5?

options: Cell D8 on the sheet named Orders
quiz.explain: Sheet name, exclamation mark, cell: D8 on Orders.

quiz.q: Where do you see the formula inside a cell?
quiz.explain: The cell shows the result; the formula bar shows the formula.

quiz.q: Which job is Excel the wrong tool for?
quiz.explain: Long documents belong in Word; Excel is for tables of facts you calculate with.

points: A **workbook** holds **worksheets**; each sheet is a grid of **cells**.
A cell address is column then row: **D4**. A range is first:last: **A1:E6**.
Excel fits any table of facts you want to sort, count or calculate.
recap.cheat: Column letter, then row number: D4. Two cells and a colon make a range: A1:E6.

cards.front: What is the difference between a workbook and a worksheet?
cards.back: The **workbook** is the file. **Worksheets** are the grids inside it, one per tab.
